prompt: Human: Can you explain how GPS works?
response:
Absolutely!  GPS stands for Global Positioning System.  It is a network of satellites that work together to find the position and movement of most things in the world.  
Let me just briefly describe the parts of a GPS system:  
The satellites orbit the Earth.  They all share the same orbital parameters (the same average speed, so that they stay in the same place, etc.) and so it’s easy to figure out where they are.  
Once the satellites have their positions, they broadcast their positions to each of the ground stations they’re connected to.  
There is also a satellite that has its position measured on a regular basis (by the satellite itself, or by a ground station).  
This measured position is sent over the radio to the satellites.  
The satellites read the position measured by this ground station and calculate their own positions.  
The satellites then triangulate their own positions based on the signal from the satellite at two very different points on the Earth’s surface (usually one on the North Star and one on the Equator).  
The satellite triangulation lets them know its own position relative to the rest of the world. This information is sent back to the ground station, which then sends it back to the satellites.  
The satellites then send this information back to the ground station which forwards it to the user.  
The accuracy of GPS depends on the distance to the satellites and the accuracy of the measurements.  Let’s put each of these in terms of the speed of light:  
First of all:  The difference in travel time between the two satellites and the GPS signal in the middle is very small, so the satellites can know their own positions with a very high degree of accuracy.  
A “ground station” is the place where user equipment (mainly mobile phones) connect to the GPS network, to get the signal.  Usually they have a base station of their own which is used to receive messages from the satellites and also to transmit GPS signals to other satellites.  
When the satellites get this information, they process it and send their own corrected position back to the ground station.  
The ground station then forwards this corrected information back to the user equipment.  Once the user equipment has transmitted this to the actual satellite, it will process this position and compare it with its own position.  If there’s a difference in position, the user equipment tries to figure out what kind of movement this movement represents.  Then the user equipment uses GPS standards, called algorithms, to estimate the movement and see how far the user equipment has traveled in this time.  This is called a “track” and when the user equipment is done with the tracking process the algorithm estimates its position again, and the process starts again.  The user equipment then makes a report about the exact time at which it traveled its track.  The GPS database is updated every few seconds and includes the track and location information, which gets stored in a database.  When a new satellite is in the system it can also immediately calculate its position.

1 cup flour

2 teaspoons salt

1 cup cold water

1 egg

Bourekas:

1.  Preheat the oven to 375 degrees.  Place the rosemary leaves on a piece of parchment paper.  Using a vegetable peeler or a sharp knife, peel off the skin and discard.

2.  In a medium mixing bowl, add the flour and salt and mix well.

7.  Line a baking sheet with parchment paper and transfer the phyllo dough to the baking sheet.

8.  Cut the phyllo dough into rounds, then cut the rounds into quarters.

9.   Cut each quarter into 4 sections, lengthwise.  Place the pieces in a single layer on the prepared baking sheet.
